en: Śrīḥ!
The Seventy Tales of the Parrot.
“Vinodinī,” accompanied by a Sanskrit-Hindi commentary.

Having prostrated before the goddess Śāradā, who is endowed with divine wisdom, I shall set forth the *Uddhāra* (Extraction) according to the tradition of the parrots (*kīra*), for the purpose of delighting the mind. (Suk 1.1)
There was a city named Candrapura;
in it there lived a king named Vikramasena.
In that city there was a merchant named Haridatta, and his wife was named Śṛṅgarasundarī.
His son was named Madanāvinoda;
his wife was Prabhāvatī,
who was the daughter of the merchant Somadatta.
But Madanavinoda was excessively attached to sensual pleasures; being a bad son, he did not heed his father’s instruction.
He was intensely addicted to gambling, hunting, prostitutes, liquor, and other such vices.
Seeing that wicked son treading the path of evil, his father Haridatta, together with his wife, became exceedingly distressed.

Seeing Haridatta afflicted by the grief of having a wicked son, his friend, a brahmin named Trivikrama, took from his own home a parrot and a maina skilled in worldly wisdom and went to his house. He said: "Friend Haridatta, protect this parrot along with its mate like a son."
"By protecting this, your sorrow will be dispelled.
Haridatta, having taken the parrot, entrusted it to his son;
Madanavinoda placed it in a golden cage within the bedchamber and nourished it.
Then once, in private, Śuka said to Madana: "O friend!
From the sorrow of your two grieving parents, streams of tears fall upon the earth."
By that evil deed, my child, you shall suffer a downfall like that of Devaśarman.
He asked, "How was that?
The parrot said: "There is a city named Pañcapura.
There lived a brahmin named Satyaśarman."
His wife was named Dharmaśīlā, and his son was Devaśarman.
Having completed his studies, he went to another country under his father’s concealment and performed austerities on the banks of the Bhāgīrathī.
Once, that ascetic sat on the bank of the Gaṅgā for the purpose of reciting prayers.
At that time, a certain crane flying overhead dropped its excrement upon his body.
The ascetic, his eyes clouded with anger, looked upward; seeing the crane fallen to the ground, consumed by the fire of his wrath, he went to the house of the Brahmin Nārāyaṇa for alms.

His wife, devoted to the service of her husband, rebuked him as he was overcome with anger and said to that bird-killer, "I am not like a crane, a fit object for your wrath. Terrified by the knowledge that his sin had been discovered and filled with wonder,
he was sent by her to the side of Dharmavyādha and went to the city of Vāraṇasī.

There, seeing him—who resembled Yama with hands smeared with blood—engaged in the sale of flesh, the hunter, who was situated within the range of her vision, first asked after her welfare and led her to his own home. There, having devoutly fed his own parents, he subsequently gave her food.
Immediately thereafter, she questioned the hunter regarding the cause of his knowledge: "How did you become so virtuous and wise?"
"And how are you wise?
The hunter replied:
"He who practices the true Dharma as handed down by his own lineage..."
He turns his back on all transformations, whether superior, inferior, or intermediate.
He is a householder, he is a sage, he is a virtuous man, he is a yogi, and he is a righteous person—
namely, that being who is constantly devoted to the service of his parents and is impartial toward all.
"Both she and I are likewise wise; yet you, having abandoned your own parents and wandering about, are not worthy of conversing with those like me. However, considering you a guest, I spoke to you.
When he had been addressed thus, that Brahmin questioned the hunter, who was full of humility.
He said:
"Those who do not worship those worthy of worship, and those who do not honor those worthy of honor—they live in reproach; they are as good as dead and do not go to heaven. (Suk 1.5)
Awakened by that hunter, he went to his own home;
he became famous in the world and a recipient of renown in the hereafter. (Suk_1.6)
"Therefore, remember the merchant's duty born of your own lineage, and be devoted to the discipline of your parents.
Thus addressed, Madana paid homage to his parents; with their permission and having taken leave of his wife, he boarded a ship and departed for another land.
Later, after his wife had spent several days in grief, she was exhorted by her independent female friends and became desirous of other men.
For they spoke thus:
"A man is a father and a kinsman only so long as he lives;
once dead, knowing him to be dead, affection ceases in an instant. (Suk_1.7)
"Therefore, since you cannot obtain your own husband, take the fruit of your youth—which will endure for only a few days—by sporting with another man.

Then, following their advice, she prepared herself for dalliance and set out to enjoy the company of another man named Guṇacandra; but as soon as she had departed, the female parrot rebuked her with words such as "Do not go!
Thereupon, as she was about to kill the parrot by wringing its neck, the bird flew away.
Then, having stood for a moment and recalled her chosen deity in her heart, she took up betel and was about to set out when the parrot said: “May there be success!
Where are you going?”—thus questioned by such words.
Taking the parrot’s words to be a mere omen, she laughed and said to him, "O King of Parrots, I have set out to experience the taste of another man.
The parrot replied, "This is indeed what ought to be done; however, it is difficult to perform and censured for women of noble family."
Furthermore, you should go at that time if you have the intelligence to do so when the contrary situation has arrived;
if you do not, then you will fall into a state of defeat.
For it is said:
Evil people are always seeking for a pretext when misfortune arrives,
just as the woman fasting for a month seized the merchant’s son by the hair.
Then, together with the courtesans, she asked with great respect; full of agitation, she said this: "What is this that has been spoken by the parrot? (Suk_1.9)
"If you have curiosity, O fair-browed one, go for the sake of others, O beautiful lady;
once you have become steady, this great story shall be heard by you afterwards. (Suk_1.10)
Having heard what the parrot said, while she sat in her own home with a mind agitated by curiosity, the parrot began a story: "There is a city named Candrāvatī.
In it dwells a king named Bhīma.
There lived a son of the merchant Mohana named Sudhana, who desired to sport with Lakṣmī, the wife of Haridatta, a resident of that same city."
Sā did not believe that;
therefore, she went to Pūrṇā, who observed the month-long fast, and having won over Pūrṇadhana, she sent her to the house as a messenger when Haridatta had gone outside the city.
She, too, propitiated Lakṣmī with flattering words.
And with a serene mind, she said, "I shall do whatever you ask. Pūrṇa replied, "In that case, accept my proposal.
She said, "This is not fitting for women of noble family; however, I shall do what I have promised before you."
And it has been said:
"Let the head be cut off, or let there be imprisonment; let fortune vanish entirely.
For the sake of fulfilling what has been promised, whatever may happen to noble men, let that be. (Suk 1.11)

"Let my head be cut off, or let there be imprisonment; let my fortune waver in every way—whatever may happen, let it happen, for the sake of fulfilling what has been undertaken by noble men. (Suk_1.11)
And so,
for horses bound by strong iron chains and various snares, the bond of speech is an even greater torment for a man of noble character. (Suk_1.12)
May there be for him the binding with various snares of firm iron chains;
yet even greater than those two is the verbal bond of a true man.
Even today, it is said that Hara does not cast off the Kālakūṭa poison;
the Tortoise indeed bears the earth upon his back;
the ocean carries the unbearable submarine fire; for the virtuous protect that which they have once undertaken. (1.13)
Hearing that, Pūrṇā was delighted and said,
"It is exactly so.
Then, having made arrangements for Lakṣmī, she led her to her own home at nightfall for the purpose of being captivated by his virtues.
Then that Mohana did not arrive before the appointed time due to being distracted by some business or other.
Thereupon, Lakṣmī, filled with desire, said, "Bring any man whatsoever.
Then the foolish Pūrṇā brought her very husband.
"When her husband has arrived, what should she do? How should she go home? Tell me, friends, or you yourselves tell her.
They replied, "We do not know;
you yourself must tell her."
The parrot said, "If you do not go, then I shall speak.
She replied, "I will not go.
The parrot, knowing that her husband was approaching even as he came, seized him by the hair and spoke thus: "O rogue!"
"You always say before me, 'You alone are my beloved, and no other woman exists for me.
But now, having been tested by me, you have been found out," she said, and she became angry.
He, however, with great difficulty and very gentle words, pacified her and led her to his own home.
Having heard the story told by the parrot, which was both terrifying and marvelous,
the merchant’s beloved wife slept that night together with a group of unchaste women.
Thus ends the first story in the Śukasaptati.
START Suk 2:
On the second day, at the onset of night, she set out together with them just as before;
having taken leave of Śuka, Śuka spoke this to her: Suk_2.1 (=15) //
"Go as you please, O fair-hipped one, if you know how to provide a reply when the time for it comes, as Yaśodevī did in her hour of crisis. (Suk_2.2 = 16)
Then Prabhāvatī asked, "Who was Yaśodevī?
When and in what difficulty did she employ such a stratagem?
Śuka replied, "If I were to tell you now, your anger at me for interrupting your pleasure would be fatal."
She said, "One must listen even to what is good or bad from friends. Having been thus permitted, Śuka said: "There is a city named Nandana;
there is a king named Nandana, and his son is Rājaśekhara."
Her daughter-in-law was Śaśiprabhā.
Upon seeing her, Dhanasena’s son, named Vīra, became filled with desire and was afflicted by a fever;
he took no food or other sustenance.
Questioned by his mother, Yaśodevī, he spoke the reason with a faltering voice: "The question was, 'That princess is difficult to obtain;
how can he live? She replied, 'You yourself must tell her.'"
Śuka said, "If you have power, then I shall tell you if you do not depart today.
When he had spoken thus, she replied, "Tell me."
Then Śuka said: "That Yaśodevī, having won over a certain bitch with food and other gifts, put on ornaments and took her along;
she went to the side of Śaśiprabhā and, in a secluded place, spoke to her with a faltering voice: 'I, you, and this [bitch] were sisters in a previous birth.'"
I fulfilled my longing for another man while free from suspicion, whereas you did so while full of suspicion;
however, she did not do so at all.
Therefore, by the power of her virtue, she has attained only the recollection of her past lives, but not wealth, and has instead been born as a female dog.
"Because of obstacles to your enjoyment, you do not possess the recollection of your past lives;
however, for me, because my enjoyments are free from obstacles, my recollection of past lives is also free from obstacles.
Therefore, out of compassion, having seen this female dog and you, I have come to speak."
Therefore, you must certainly grant whatever is desired by those who come as supplicants;
for he who practices giving shall become the abode of all prosperity.
And it has been said:
They speak but do not beg; subsisting on alms, they go from house to house, saying: "Let it be given constantly to those in need; such is the fruit for one who does not give. (Suk_2.3 = 17)
Then Śaśiprabhā, weeping while clinging to her neck, said, "O auspicious lady, unite me as well with another man.
Thereupon Yaśodevī, having comforted her and informed her husband, led her to her own home and united her with her son.

And that Rājaśekhara, satisfied by the gift of wealth and other things, did not prevent her, thinking, "She is my friend. Thus, O beautiful lady, having deceived both the prince and the princess, Yaśodēvī accomplished her own purpose through great intelligence. (Suk_2.4 = 18)
If you have this intention, O fair-browed one, go then to the presence of him;
enjoy sleep, O large-eyed one, do not otherwise mock yourself. (Suk_2.5 = 19)
Having heard this story of the parrot, Prabhāvatī fell asleep. Thus ends the second story in the *Śukasaptati*.
START Suk 3: Then on another day, Prabhāvatī asks the parrot. The parrot says:
"Go, O King; what wonder is there where your mind finds delight? If you know how to protect yourself, do so like a king. (Suk_3.1 = 20)
Prabhāvatī asks: "How was that? Śuka relates: "There is a city named Viśālā;
there, King Sudarśana reigned."

In that place there was a merchant named Vimala, who had two wives, both fortunate and endowed with beauty. Seeing them, a rogue named Kuṭila, desiring to seize those two wives, propitiated the goddess Ambikā and requested her own form [of Vimala].
Having obtained that nature, when Vimala had gone outside, he went to his house and took control.

Having brought the entire circle of his attendants under his influence through gifts of grace and wealth, he enjoys himself at his own pleasure, having satisfied his two wives with honors, gifts, and the like.
His attendants constantly reflect: "This Vimala has become a donor after hearing of the impermanence of wealth and other such things."
Then Satyavimala also arrived at the gate, but was turned away by the gatekeeper at the command of Kuṭilā.
Standing outside, he cried out, "I have been deceived by the king of rogues!
As he was thus lamenting, the people of his clan gathered there out of curiosity.
At that moment, the merchant caravan abandoned the marketplaces and gathered together, crying out before the chief guards and ministers:
"O King, I have been deceived by a king of rogues!
Thereupon, the king dispatched men to investigate the matter.
He, too, made them favorable by giving them wealth and other gifts.
Seeing that giver of wealth in his house, the people said: "Master, Vimala is at home, and this king of rogues is standing at the door."
Thereupon, the king placed both of them together in one place;
consequently, no one among the two could distinguish between the rogue and the honest man.
A great clamor arose, causing the ruin of all worldly affairs and bringing reproach upon the king.
For the restraint of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous by kings leads to heaven.
And it has been said:
"The fire produced from the heat of the oppression of subjects [consumes the king]."
Without having consumed the king’s lineage, his fortune, and his life, the fire does not turn back.
Then the king reflected on how to reach a decision between the two in private.

This was his question: "Tell me, how can a certainty be reached? Śuka said: That king, having found a means, placed those two wives of Vimala separately and asked them: "At your marriage, what wealth or ornament was given to you by your husband?"
And what was spoken later? What was the conversation during the first meeting? Who was the husband? Who was the mother? And who was the father?
"What is your family? What is your caste?"—
when asked thus, they both told everything exactly as it was obtained, exactly as it had occurred, exactly as it had been spoken, and exactly as it had been slept.
Thereafter, those two men were questioned; as they contradicted one another,
the king declared that he who spoke in accordance with the agreement between his two wives, named Rukmiṇī and Sundarī, was the truth-teller,
while the other was a rogue and was banished by the king.
"But Satya, having been honored by the king along with his wife, went to his own home.
Thus was the thought of the great king.
Having heard this story, Prabhāvatī fell asleep.
Thus ends the third story in the Śukasaptati.
START Suk 4:
Then, on another occasion, Prabhāvatī asked the parrot.
The parrot said: “Do not go away after having treated me with contempt.”

"O Goddess, beneficial words should be accepted even from a child. In the past, a Brahmin who showed contempt and turned his back on the advice of the elders fell into misfortune by marrying a poison-maiden. (Suk_4.1 = 22)
Prabhāvatī asked, “How was that?
The parrot said: “There is a Brahmin settlement named Somaprabha.
There lived a learned and righteous Brahmin named Somaśarman.”
Her daughter, endowed with beauty, nobility, and virtue, was known as a "poison-maiden" (*viṣakanyā*).
Because of that fear, no one would marry her.
Then Somaśarman, wandering the earth in search of a bridegroom, arrived at a settlement of brahmins named Janasthāna.
In that place, there was a Brahmin named Govinda who was dull-witted and destitute;
he was given a maiden in marriage.
Despite the protests of his friends, he disregarded their warnings and married a "deluding poison-maiden" (mohinī viṣakanyā) who was endowed with every beauty, grace, and virtue.
She was clever, whereas Govinda was foolish and young in age;
consequently, she lamented her own beauty, grace, and youth,
thinking that an unrefined husband is no match for women.
A leader who lacks virtue for those who are mature, and meager wealth for those who are virtuous and generous—this causes suffering. (Suk_4.2 = 23)
Fasting during the rainy season, poverty on the day of youth, and the loss of first affection—these three are all heavy sufferings. (Suk_4.3 = 24)
Living abroad during the rainy season, poverty on the day of one's youth, and separation from a first love—these three are heavy sorrows. (Suk_4.24)
Reciting when there is no occasion, singing a song devoid of melody, and claiming "no, no" during sexual union—these three are grave misfortunes. (Suk_4.4 = 25)
A song recited out of context, singing without a voice,
and sexual pleasure while saying "no, no"— these three are heavy sufferings.
On another occasion, she said to her husband Govinda, “Many days have passed since I arrived from my father’s house;
therefore, I shall go only with you and no other way.
Then, having sought out a cart, he set out together with his wife.
As she was traveling along the path, she met a certain young Brahmin named Viṣṇu, who was eloquent, handsome, and brave.
Mutual passion arose between that Brahmin and her.
And it is said: "First there is affection arising from sight and such; then follows the state of mental attachment and the formation of intentions."

The loss of sleep, emaciation of the body, turbidity of the senses, cessation of their functions, the destruction of shame, madness, fainting, and death—these are the states to which the world is reduced by the arrows of the Flower-Bowed One; may that Madana, who has cast aside all other archers, be victorious! (Suk_4.5 = 26)
That traveler gives a heap of betel leaves to the couple;
thus, the village Brahmin Rohaviṣṇu, having gained their trust, and having escaped the fear of his own imprisonment and attachment, mounts the vehicle of the traveler.
And while her husband has gone behind a tree, Viṣṇu enjoys that deluded woman, bringing her under his own control.
She informed him of her own name, lineage, and family history;
and when her husband arrived, she forbade him from mounting the cart, saying, "You are a thief.
Viṣṇu, having seized her, overpowered Govinda.
Then a hair-to-hair struggle ensued between the two.
Govinda, however, was defeated by Viṣṇu through the power of the poison-maiden. Then, taking her with him, Viṣṇu set out for his own home.
Govinda, standing behind him near a village on the road, went there and cried out: "This thief has seized my wife! Save her!
O people, I come to you for refuge!"
Then Viṣṇu was seized by the village headman along with Mohinī.
When questioned, Viṣṇu gave this reply: "I have married her;
moreover, this traveler saw my wife on the road and became infatuated with her."
When Govinda was also questioned, he gave this very same answer.
Then the minister, having heard the identical response from both of them, asked about their caste and so forth.
[The king said: "But since all three agree, how can there be a certainty?"
Thus ends the question of Śuka.
Then, being questioned by her, Śuka said: "The minister asked, 'How many days will it take for you to set out on your journey?'"
They replied, “The meeting took place this morning after the meal.
Then the minister questioned the two brahmins individually: “What did she eat at the time of her meal this morning? Govinda knew what she had eaten, but the other did not.
Then, having been thus mocked by his minister, Goninda was instructed:
"Fie on this Brahmin woman, who brings suffering both in this world and the next; release her quickly!"
And it is said:

The wise abandon a physician addicted to drink, an actor who has poorly studied his part, a wandering mendicant who is a fool, a warrior who is a coward, a lecher who is past his prime, a twice-born man devoid of Vedic study, a kingdom lacking a young king and a minister, a friend who seeks out one's faults, and a wife who is proud of her youth and devoted to another. (Suk_4.6 = 27)
Nevertheless, though censured by the virtuous at that time for his greed for a lustful woman, he set out taking her with him; for her sake, he was slain on the road. (Suk_4.7 = 28)
Therefore, O Queen, he who— though instructed by his elders— acts with such contempt,
meets with defeat, just like the Brahmin Govinda.
Having heard this story, Prabhāvatī fell asleep.
Thus ends the fourth story in the Śukasaptati.
START SUK 5: On another day, she asks Śuka about going. Śuka says:
Go, O Goddess; you shall know how to provide an answer in the king’s assembly, just as a clever girl did in a difficult situation. (Suk_5.1 = 30)
Questioned by Prabhāvatī, the parrot told this story: "There is a city named Ujjayinī. There, King Vikramāditya reigned.
To that king was born a daughter named Kāmalīlā, born of a noble family."
And she was exceedingly dear to the king.
Once, while the king was eating with her, he had fried fish served to her.
She said, "My lord,"
"I am not even capable of looking at these men, let alone touching them.
Having heard this, the fish laughed with such a loud, boisterous laugh that it was heard throughout the city.
The king, seeking the cause of that laughter of the fish, questioned his ministers, astrologers, and experts in the science of omens.

When no one knew [the reason], he said to the family priest, the foremost of all the twice-born: "The cause of the fish's laughter must be told by you alone; otherwise, you shall be banished from this country.
Having heard these words, the priest requested a delay of five days and returned home despondent. Not knowing the answer, that priest feared he would be banished before the king.

The question is: "How can he become so? Śuka also provides the answer: That Brahmin, overcome with despondency, was addressed by his daughter Bālapaṇḍitā: "Father, why do you appear as if your mind is distressed?"
Tell me the cause of your despondency;
even in adversity, the wise should remain steadfast.
And it has been said:
Rarely does a mother give birth to a son who is the ornament of the three worlds—one who feels no joy in prosperity, no dejection in adversity, and no fear in battle. (Suk 5.2 = 31)
Then the Brahmin related the events in detail: "For this reason, the king is banishing me from the city;
for—there is no friendship, no trust, no affection, and no kinship [with those who oppose one's interests]."
Why should one have any association with anyone else in this saṃsāra, especially with a king who seeks only deception?
And it is said:

"Purity in a crow, truthfulness in a gambler, patience in a serpent, the subduing of lust in women, steadfastness in a eunuch, and reflection on reality in a drunkard—where has a king who is a friend ever been seen or heard of? (Suk_5.4 = 33)
Furthermore: One should never place trust in rivers, in clawed beasts, in horned animals, in those with weapons in hand, in women, or in royal courts. (Suk_5.5 = 34)
Kings are like serpents: they possess wealth, are clad in their royal robes, are cruel, move with crooked gait, and are difficult to approach because of their inherent danger.
Even while smiling, a king kills; even while showing honor, a wicked person kills;
even while touching, an elephant kills; even while merely smelling, a serpent kills.
This king, though served by me since childhood, has become hostile toward me;
therefore, desiring to live, I must go to a foreign land together with the twice-born.
And it is said:
One should abandon an individual for the sake of a family; one should abandon a family for the sake of a village;
one should abandon a village for the sake of a country; and one should abandon the entire earth for the sake of the self.
Then, having heard her father’s words, the girl said: "Father, what you have said is right;
however, for those who are without a master, there is no worship anywhere."
As it has been said:
"One who is not prominent may become prominent if he serves a king;
even one who is prominent may become unimportant if he is devoid of service. (Suk 5.9 = 38)
A king favors the person who is merely close at hand, even if that person lacks learning, noble birth, or prior acquaintance;
for generally, rulers, women, and climbing vines entwine themselves around whoever is situated by their side. (Suk_5.10 = 39)
The messengers of death slowly ascend even upon a king who shakes them off;
staying close at hand, they examine the objects of his anger and his favor.
And so it is said:

For those possessed of learning, for the great-souled, for those distinguished by their artistic skill and prowess, and for those who know the way of service—none of these have a refuge other than a king. (Suk_5.12 = 41)
Those who, despite possessing great energy for [their] birth and so forth, do not approach the king, for them begging alms until death is prescribed as the penance. (Suk_5.13 = 42)

O dear one, he who, being dull-witted in his actions, does not understand the diseases, the planetary influences, the human rulers, or the means [to counter them], is certainly not stable. (Suk_5.14 = 43)
And it has been said:
"When snakes, tigers, elephants, and lions have been brought under control by means of skillful methods, what small matter is a king to the wise who are free from negligence? (Suk 5.15 = 44)
And so it is said:
"Only by relying upon a king does a learned man attain supreme eminence;
without the Malaya mountain, sandalwood does not flourish elsewhere. (Suk 5.16 = 45)
When the king is gracious, there are white parasols, delightful horses, and elephants ever in rut. (Suk_5.17 = 46)
Therefore, dear father, you are honored by the king and a recipient of his favor;
thus, do not despair in this matter of doubt. For:

When Rājagṛha was reached during a difficult time of uncertainty regarding affairs, the chief ministers were the dispellers of doubt for the kings whose minds were filled with suspicion. (Suk_5.18 = 47)
"Therefore, my dear father,
remain steadfast;
after the Fish's laughter, I shall speak before the King."
"Bathe and eat.
Having done so, he went before the king and reported everything;
the king, being pleased, summoned her.
Having bestowed her blessing, she said to the king: "O King, do not mock the Brahmins in vain.
Have you ever seen or heard of such a ridiculous thing regarding fish?
How is it that you are not ashamed to question me, a woman of no strength?"
For: Even another king who bears a divine form is not truly extraordinary;
you, however, O scorcher of foes, are Vikramāditya in the truest sense of the name.
And it has been said:

"Having taken sovereignty from Indra, majesty from Agni, wrath from Yama, and wealth from Vaiśravaṇa, as well as the steadfastness of character from Rāma and Janārdana, the body of a king is fashioned. (Suk_5.20 = 49)
And so it is said in the *Mahābhārata*:

"O Vṛkodara, do not strike with your foot the commander of eleven armies—he who was the lord even of the five [Pāṇḍavas], yet possessed the nature of a mere mortal. (Suk_5.21 = 50) [Note: Some manuscripts read 'māninā' instead of 'mānavī'].
"O Lord, why do you not investigate this yourself?
For you alone are the dispeller of all doubts. If, however, there is a desire to hear it from others, then listen."
"O King, this queen, being a great satī, does not touch these fish; because they were addressed by the name 'man,' the fish have surely laughed. (Suk_5.22 = 51)
O King, you should always contemplate this meaning of the verse in your heart; otherwise, O Lord, if you, being of dull intellect, question me again, [it will be fruitless]. (Suk_5.23 = 52)
O King, how could there be any suspicion of unchastity in the queen who had not seen the sun?
Regarding both the meaning of the verse and the matter at hand, even the wise kings, though experts in all matters, do not understand why the fish are laughing. (Suk_5.24 = 53)
Then, seeing the assembly bewildered, Bālapaṇḍitā rose and departed.
Śuka also said, "I shall speak tomorrow morning.
Having heard these words of the parrot, Prabhāvatī went to sleep.
Thus ends the fifth story in the Śukasaptati.
START Suk 6:
Then, on another day, Prabhāvatī said to the parrot:
